extracted.intended_audience: graduate students or advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry / readers of Vakil's Foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and exercises introducing spectral sequences (from double complexes) and the basic theory of presheaves and sheaves, with concrete examples (sheaf of smooth functions) and categorical remarks. Contains definitions, examples, and exercises used to build facility with these tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernels commute with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two diagrams a, b : I → C and a natural transformation h : a ⇒ b in an abelian category C, the kernels ker(h_i) form another diagram indexed by I and there is a canonical isomorphism lim ker(h_i) ≅ ker(lim a_i → lim b_i), assuming the limits exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.6.J: describe canonical isomorphism and use that kernels are limits; this is an instance of how limits interact with kernel constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits commute with limits (general statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sense of the statement that 'limits commute with limits' in a general category and prove it. (Hint: kernels are limits so Exercise 1.6.J should be a corollary.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.6.K: interpret limits as functors and show composition/commutation properties; use kernel-as-limit observations as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right adjoints commute with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If (F : C → D, G : D → C) is an adjoint pair and A = lim_i A_i is a limit in D of a diagram indexed by I, then G(A) = lim_i G(A_i) (with corresponding maps) in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 1.6.16: proof via universal property and adjointness; dual statements hold for left adjoints and colimits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoint functors and exactness in abelian categories
rubrics_metrics.description: If F and G are additive functors between abelian categories with (F, G) an adjoint pair, then G is left-exact and F is right-exact (since kernels are limits and cokernels are colimits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relationship between (co)kernels and (co)limits to read off exactness properties of adjoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered colimits are exact in 'sets with additional structure' (e.g., ModA)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ModA (and more generally in any abelian category whose objects can be interpreted as 'sets with additional structure'), colimits over filtered index categories are exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.6.L: right-exactness follows from adjoint discussion; left-exactness can be shown by checking that localization or stalkification is exact (see hints referencing Exercise 1.6.G(a) and Exercise 2.6.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtered colimits commute with homology (FHHF)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filtered colimits commute with homology in ModA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.6.M: use the FHHF Theorem (Exercise 1.6.I) and the previous exercise; think about how limits/colimits commute with homology and which way maps go.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exactness of inverse limit under surjective transition maps (Mittag–Leffler style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an inverse system of exact sequences of modules ... with the transition maps on the left term An+1 → An surjective, the limit sequence 0 → lim An → lim Bn → lim Cn → 0 is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.6.N: define the maps in the limit sequence carefully and use surjectivity of transitions to ensure exactness at the left term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample: exact functors need not commute with all colimits
rubrics_metrics.description: Right-exact functors do not always commute with colimits; e.g., the 'double dual' functor V ↦ V^{∨∨} is covariant and right-exact (in fact exact) but does not commute with infinite direct sums: (⊕_{i=1}^∞ k)^{∨∨} is not isomorphic to ⊕_{i=1}^∞ (k^{∨∨}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unimportant Remark 1.6.17: be cautious about generalizing finite-sum behavior to infinite sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation for derived functors from left-exact functors
rubrics_metrics.description: When you see a left-exact functor F, you should 'dream' there is a long exact sequence continuing FM' → FM → FM'' → R^1F(M') → ...; the next term depends only on M' and is denoted R^1F(M'). In good cases such a continuation (derived functors) exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 1.6.18: this is the conceptual motivation for derived functors; think long exact sequences and vanishing of R^1F causing surjectivity of FM → FM''.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a double complex
rubrics_metrics.description: A double complex is a collection of A-modules E^{p,q} with 'rightward' morphisms d: E^{p,q} → E^{p+1,q} and 'upward' morphisms d: E^{p,q} → E^{p,q+1}, satisfying d^2 = 0 in each direction and either commuting or anticommute in squares (convention: anticommute here).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.1: note conventions about indexing, signs (replace d by (-1)^p d to switch commuting/anticommuting), and variations (vertical arrows downward, some E^{p,q} zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the total (single) complex from a double complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the total complex E^k = ⊕_i E^{i,k-i} (the kth anti-diagonal) with differential d = d_h + d_v (with signs as needed); then d^2 = 0 and the cohomology of this single complex is the hypercohomology of the double complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.1: understand the grading conventions and that total complex cohomology is the invariant computed by spectral sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate definition of a spectral sequence (pages, differentials, and stabilization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A spectral sequence (rightward orientation) is a sequence of tables/pages E^{p,q}_r for r = 0,1,2,... with differentials d_r : E^{p,q}_r → E^{p-r+1,q+r}_r satisfying d_r ∘ d_r = 0 and such that E^{p,q}_{r+1} ≅ H(E^{p,q}_r, d_r). Each E^{p,q}_r is a subquotient of E^{p,q}_i for i < r, and for bounded/bounded-below conditions the terms stabilize to E^{p,q}_∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.2: orientation determines which differentials are 'horizontal' vs 'vertical'; visualize maps and degrees; check stabilization in first quadrant or finite-row situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of first pages: E0, E1, E2
rubrics_metrics.description: E0 is the table of the original double complex (rows/columns as complexes); d0 is the rightward differential. E1 is the table of cohomologies of rows (take cohomology with respect to d0), and d1 is induced by the vertical maps on row cohomology, making columns into complexes. E2 is cohomology of (E1, d1) and the pattern continues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.2: explicitly compute d0, d1, d2 by hand for double complexes; Exercise 1.7.A gives concrete identifications for low-degree cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence/abutment and filtration of H^k(total complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a filtration of H^k(E•) with subquotients given by E^{p,k-p}_∞. In favorable cases (e.g., first quadrant double complex) for fixed p,q the terms E^{p,q}_r stabilize and define E^{p,q}_∞, and the spectral sequence 'converges' or 'abuts' to H^•(E•).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formula (1.7.2.2) and accompanying explanation: understand which entries become subobjects vs quotients by following orientation and later-page differentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation duality: horizontal vs vertical start gives different filtrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting the spectral sequence with horizontal vs vertical differentials yields two spectral sequences (rightward vs upward orientation) that both compute H^•(E•) but give filtrations in opposite orders; in general there is no canonical isomorphism between the two pages E^{p,q}_∞ and the oppositely oriented ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.3: use whichever orientation gives easier computation; the two algorithms compute the same total cohomology but reveal different pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spectral sequences to derive classical diagram lemmas (Snake Lemma example)
rubrics_metrics.description: By fitting a suitable double complex into the spectral sequence machinery and comparing the two orientations, one can derive the Snake Lemma exact sequence 0 → ker α → ker β → ker γ → coker α → coker β → coker γ → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 1.7.5: compute with rightward orientation (rows exact → immediate vanishing) and upward orientation (columns give kernel/cokernel entries) to deduce exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spectral sequences to prove Five Lemma variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectral sequence computations (choosing orientation to force many zeros) yield proofs of the Five Lemma and subtler variants where some maps are only injective or surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 1.7.6 and Exercises 1.7.C–D: practice producing which entries must vanish and read off consequences for the middle map being an isomorphism/injection/surjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping cone and long exact sequence in homology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a morphism of complexes µ : A• → B•, the mapping cone C• is the total complex of the associated double complex and there is a long exact sequence ... → H^{i-1}(C•) → H^i(A•) → H^i(B•) → H^i(C•) → H^{i+1}(A•) → ... . In particular, µ induces isomorphism on cohomology iff the mapping cone is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.7.E: indexing conventions may vary; this is the standard homological algebra fact used often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short exact sequence of complexes induces long exact sequence in cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: A short exact sequence of complexes gives a long exact sequence in cohomology; spectral sequences can be used to prove this generalization (Theorem 1.6.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 1.7.F: view as an application of mapping cone or spectral sequence machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality of spectral sequences in the 0th page
rubrics_metrics.description: The spectral sequence formalism is functorial in the 0th page: spectral sequences have good functorial properties in the underlying double complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 1.7.7: note that constructions and proofs show how maps of double complexes induce maps of associated spectral sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a presheaf (as a contravariant functor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A presheaf F on a topological space X assigns to each open set U ⊂ X a set F(U) and to each inclusion V ⊂ U a restriction map res_{U,V}: F(U) → F(V), satisfying res_{U,U} = id and functoriality res_{W,V} ∘ res_{V,U} = res_{W,U}. Equivalently, a presheaf is a contravariant functor from the category of open sets of X to Sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 2.2.2 and Exercise 2.2.A: several notations exist (F(U), Γ(U,F), H^0(U,F)). This viewpoint is useful for categorical manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of stalks and germs; stalk as colimit
rubrics_metrics.description: The stalk F_p at p is the set of germs: pairs (f,U) with p ∈ U, modulo identification when they agree on some smaller neighborhood. Equivalently F_p = colim_{p ∈ U} F(U) (filtered colimit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections 2.2.3–2.2.5: think of germs as 'shreds' of sections near p; both concrete and colimit definitions are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a sheaf: identity (separated) and gluability axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: A presheaf F is a sheaf if for every open cover {U_i} of U: (Identity) if f,g ∈ F(U) satisfy f|_{U_i} = g|_{U_i} for all i then f = g; (Gluability) if given sections f_i ∈ F(U_i) with f_i|_{U_i∩U_j} = f_j|_{U_i∩U_j} there exists f ∈ F(U) with f|_{U_i} = f_i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition 2.2.6: identity = 'at most one' gluing; gluability = 'at least one' gluing. For valued-in-categories note F(∅) is final object (follows from axioms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf axioms as equalizer/limit/exactness
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity and gluability axioms can be interpreted as exactness of the 'equalizer exact sequence' F(U) → ∏_i F(U_i) ⇉ ∏_{i,j} F(U_i ∩ U_j) (identity = exactness at F(U), gluability = exactness at ∏_i F(U_i)). Equivalently F(∪_i U_i) is a certain limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2.2.7 and Exercise 2.2.C: this categorical viewpoint clarifies sheaf conditions as a gluing/limit condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheaf of smooth functions example: restriction, uniqueness on covers, and gluing
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sheaf O of smooth functions on X = ℝ^n: restrictions res_{V,U}: O(U) → O(V) exist; if two functions agree on an open cover they are equal; if functions on each U_i agreeing on overlaps can be glued to a global smooth function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2.1 motivating example: same properties hold for continuous, real-analytic, and various 'nice' function classes; this motivates the sheaf axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalks of sheaf of smooth functions are local rings and mp/m^2 relates to cotangent space
rubrics_metrics.description: For the sheaf O of smooth functions, the stalk O_p is a local ring with maximal ideal m_p consisting of germs vanishing at p; O_p/m_p ≅ ℝ. Moreover m_p/m_p^2 is naturally the cotangent space at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 2.1.1 and 2.1.2: Exercise 2.1.A shows uniqueness of maximal ideal and invertibility outside it; differential-geometric readers should verify cotangent identification.
